sources.text: Introduction, objectives and overview of the overall research programme Despite rapid advances, the current state of AI in healthcare remains correlation-driven, fragmented and poorly adapted to clinical reality. Most deployed models operate as statistical predictors rather than decision technologies and therefore struggle with external validity, transportability and regulatory acceptance. Systematic reviews confirm that adoption is slowed by fragmented data environments, limited explainability and a lack of prospective clinical evidence. In cardiovascular applications, the literature reveals broad enthusiasm but few implementation case studies and no clear pathways for compliance with emerging AI regulations. This leaves hospitals, regulators and patients with "AI as a promise" rather than a demonstrably safe and auditable intervention tool. The proposal is timely because emerging regulatory and policy frameworks now require trustworthy, explainable and interoperable AI in high-risk healthcare settings. PROJECT-X directly responds to these policy drivers while contributing to broader digital-health and societal objectives through fair, robust AI tools that are clinically actionable across diverse populations. PROJECT-X’s overarching ambition is: 1. to replace correlation-centric models with causal objectives and counterfactual evaluation; 2. to treat interoperability and governance as first-class design constraints; 3. to embed human-in-the-loop co-creation and targeted stakeholder training; 4. to execute healthcare-embedded case studies that generate evidence on safety, adoption and value. Together, these elements define a cohesive research programme addressing key skills and knowledge gaps in healthcare AI. Specific measurable research and innovation objectives O1 – Trustworthy causal AI (WP1) Develop explainable, fair and sensitivity-aware causal AI models that articulate assumptions, quantify uncertainty and provide counterfactual “what-if” and cause- effect reasoning at both patient and policy levels. Success KPIs • KPI1.1: ≥1 multimodal AI model integrated with causal modules.

sources.text: Global health and policy roadmaps call for AI systems that are safe, interoperable and implementable in real-world healthcare environments. Yet adoption consistently stalls because of privacy concerns, interoperability challenges, bias, trust deficits and implementation barriers. PROJECT-X addresses these challenges through causal objectives, governance-ready engineering and healthcare-embedded validation, directly targeting gaps identified by healthcare-system stakeholders and implementation-science studies. The programme responds to calls for organisation-wide strategies and enabling infrastructures capable of supporting trustworthy AI deployment beyond isolated research pilots. It also aligns with recent analyses emphasising resilience to variability, uncertainty and distribution shifts in healthcare data. By embedding regulatory requirements such as AI governance frameworks, medical- device regulations, data-protection requirements and interoperability standards into the research process, the project goes beyond conventional AI prototypes and instead develops conformity-ready documentation, monitoring pipelines and implementation frameworks suitable for reuse by healthcare providers and industrial stakeholders. Beyond the state of the art: scientific and technical innovations The proposed innovations build upon and extend recent advances in causal explainability, federated learning, multimodal AI and trustworthy clinical decision support. 1. Causal, multimodal and federated AI The programme develops multimodal causal models and federated transportability methodologies capable of supporting robust effect estimation across institutions. The research integrates: • longitudinal healthcare records, • medical imaging, • physiological measurements, • biomarker information, • patient-generated health data, into semantically harmonised and privacy-preserving analytical frameworks.

sources.text: Overall methodology We adopt a highly interdisciplinary and strongly collaborative approach that prioritises early and open exchange of ideas within the consortium and with the wider community. Our overarching ambition is to replace correlation-driven pipelines with causal AI systems that are resilient to real-world data challenges, interoperable across heterogeneous healthcare infrastructures and regulatory compliant. The programme balances fundamental research with applied validation in healthcare environments, ensuring that methods remain theoretically rigorous, technically auditable and practically implementable in routine healthcare. This framework is underpinned by four methodological advances. Causal AI and counterfactual reasoning Instead of relying solely on black-box prediction, the programme develops models capable of estimating cause-effect relationships and counterfactual outcomes. The models explicitly encode assumptions and quantify both structural and statistical uncertainty. This directly addresses important reproducibility, robustness and bias challenges identified in healthcare AI. Regulatory-grade pipelines Compliance with healthcare AI regulations and governance frameworks is treated as a methodological requirement rather than a post hoc constraint. Risk classification, transparency, robustness, human oversight and lifecycle monitoring are embedded throughout the development process within a quality-managed framework. The methodology operationalises major regulatory requirements relevant to high-risk healthcare AI systems, including medical-device, data-governance and AI-governance obligations.

sources.text: Introduction, objectives and overview of the overall research programme Despite rapid advances, the current state of AI in healthcare remains correlation-driven, fragmented and poorly adapted to clinical reality. Most deployed models operate as statistical predictors rather than decision technologies and therefore struggle with external validity, transportability and regulatory acceptance. Systematic reviews confirm that adoption is slowed by fragmented data environments, limited explainability and a lack of prospective clinical evidence. In cardiovascular applications, the literature reveals broad enthusiasm but few implementation case studies and no clear pathways for compliance with emerging AI regulations. This leaves hospitals, regulators and patients with "AI as a promise" rather than a demonstrably safe and auditable intervention tool. The proposal is timely because emerging regulatory and policy frameworks now require trustworthy, explainable and interoperable AI in high-risk healthcare settings. PROJECT-X directly responds to these policy drivers while contributing to broader digital-health and societal objectives through fair, robust AI tools that are clinically actionable across diverse populations. PROJECT-X’s overarching ambition is: 1. to replace correlation-centric models with causal objectives and counterfactual evaluation; 2. to treat interoperability and governance as first-class design constraints; 3. to embed human-in-the-loop co-creation and targeted stakeholder training; 4. to execute healthcare-embedded case studies that generate evidence on safety, adoption and value. Together, these elements define a cohesive research programme addressing key skills and knowledge gaps in healthcare AI. Specific measurable research and innovation objectives O1 – Trustworthy causal AI (WP1) Develop explainable, fair and sensitivity-aware causal AI models that articulate assumptions, quantify uncertainty and provide counterfactual “what-if” and cause- effect reasoning at both patient and policy levels. Success KPIs • KPI1.1: ≥1 multimodal AI model integrated with causal modules.

sources.text: Overall methodology We adopt a highly interdisciplinary and strongly collaborative approach that prioritises early and open exchange of ideas within the consortium and with the wider community. Regulatory-grade pipelines Compliance with healthcare AI regulations and governance frameworks is treated as a methodological requirement rather than a post hoc constraint. Risk classification, transparency, robustness, human oversight and lifecycle monitoring are embedded throughout the development process within a quality-managed framework. The methodology operationalises major regulatory requirements relevant to high-risk healthcare AI systems, including medical-device, data-governance and AI-governance obligations.
